paragraphs: I shall be told that Christian troops are excellent. I deny it. Show me an example. For my part, I know of no Christian troops. I shall be told of the Crusades. Without disputing the courage of the Crusaders, I answer that, far from being Christians, they were the priests’ soldiers, citizens of the Church. They fought for their spiritual country, which the Church had somehow made into a temporal one. Properly understood, this goes back to paganism: since the Gospel sets up no national religion, a holy war is impossible among Christians.

Under the pagan emperors, the Christian soldiers were brave. Every Christian writer says so, and I believe it: it was a case of honorable rivalry with the pagan troops. As soon as the emperors became Christian, this rivalry no longer existed, and when the Cross had driven out the eagle, Roman valor disappeared entirely.

But let us set political considerations aside and come back to what is right, and settle our principles on this important point. The right that the social compact gives the Sovereign over the subjects does not, as we have seen, go beyond the limits of public expediency.[5] The subjects therefore owe the Sovereign an account of their opinions only to the extent that those opinions matter to the community. Now, it matters very much to the community that each citizen have a religion. That will make him love his duty. But the dogmas of that religion concern the State and its members only insofar as they relate to morality and to the duties that the person who professes them is bound to perform for others. Beyond that, each man may hold whatever opinions he pleases, and the Sovereign has no business taking notice of them. For the Sovereign has no authority in the other world; whatever the lot of its subjects may be in the life to come, that is not its concern, provided they are good citizens in this life.

There is therefore a purely civil profession of faith, whose articles the Sovereign should fix, not exactly as religious dogmas but as social sentiments, without which a man cannot be a good citizen or a faithful subject.[6] The Sovereign can compel no one to believe them, but it can banish from the State anyone who does not believe them. It can banish him, not for impiety, but as an anti-social being, incapable of truly loving the laws and justice, and of sacrificing his life to his duty when necessary. If anyone, after publicly acknowledging these dogmas, behaves as if he does not believe them, let him be punished by death: he has committed the worst of all crimes, that of lying before the law.

The dogmas of civil religion ought to be few, simple and precisely worded, without explanation or commentary. These are its positive dogmas: the existence of a mighty, intelligent and beneficent Divinity, who has foresight and providence; the life to come; the happiness of the just; the punishment of the wicked; the sanctity of the social compact and the laws. Its negative dogmas I limit to one: intolerance, which belongs to the forms of worship we have rejected.

Those who distinguish civil intolerance from theological intolerance are, in my view, mistaken. The two are inseparable. It is impossible to live at peace with people we regard as damned; to love them would be to hate God, who punishes them. We positively must either bring them back or torment them. Wherever theological intolerance is accepted, it must inevitably have some civil effect;[7] and as soon as it has such an effect, the Sovereign is no longer Sovereign, even in temporal matters. From then on the priests are the real masters, and kings are only their ministers.

Now that there is no longer, and can no longer be, an exclusive national religion, tolerance should be given to all religions that tolerate others, so long as their dogmas contain nothing contrary to the duties of citizenship. But whoever dares to say _Outside the Church there is no salvation_ ought to be driven from the State, unless the State is the Church and the prince is the pontiff. Such a dogma is good only in a theocratic government; in any other it is fatal. The reason for which Henry IV is said to have embraced the Roman religion ought to make every honest man leave it, and still more any prince who knows how to reason.

Is it not clear that, in establishing the authority of the Church in this respect, it will be destroying that of the prince, who will from then on have only as many subjects as the clergy choose to allow him? The Church will be in a position to marry or not to marry people, according to their acceptance of this or that doctrine, their admission or rejection of this or that formula, their greater or lesser piety. By the exercise of prudence and firmness, the Church alone will therefore dispose of all inheritances, offices and citizens, and even of the State itself, which could not subsist if it were composed entirely of bastards. But, I shall be told, there will be appeals on the ground of abuse, summonses and decrees; the Church’s temporal property will be seized. How sad! The clergy, if it has even a little — I will not say courage, but sense — will take no notice and go its way. It will quietly allow appeals, summonses, decrees and seizures, and in the end it will remain the master. It is not, I think, a great sacrifice to give up a part when one is sure of securing the whole.
